title: Sagas and Distributed Transactions
summary: Once the data lives in separate services there is no shared transaction to roll back. A saga replaces atomicity with a sequence of local commits, each paired with a compensating action that semantically undoes it — and the system is visibly half-finished in between.
analogy: Booking a holiday across three separate websites: flight, hotel, car. Each booking is final the moment you click, and there is no button that unbooks all three. If the car falls through you do not rewind time — you cancel the hotel, which may keep a fee, and you email the airline for a refund that arrives next week. In between, you genuinely have a flight and no car, and anyone looking at your calendar sees that half-finished state.

explanation.beginner: Inside one database, a transaction gives you all-or-nothing for free: either every change happens or none does. Split your data across an order service, a payment service and an inventory service, and that guarantee disappears — each one commits to its own database, and there is no shared undo. A saga is the workaround. You run the steps one at a time, and for each step you write a second operation that undoes it in business terms: if payment succeeded but stock ran out, you issue a refund. The refund is not a rollback — the charge really happened and the customer really saw it — but the end state is correct.
explanation.interview: The loss is atomicity across service boundaries. Two-phase commit restores it with prepare/commit, but participants hold locks for the whole round trip and a coordinator crash after prepare leaves them blocked with no way to decide — 2PC buys atomicity with availability, which most systems refuse. A saga is instead a sequence of local ACID transactions T1..Tn with compensations C1..Cn-1; on failure at step k you run Ck-1..C1 in reverse. Consequences to name: no isolation, so intermediate states are readable (dirty reads, lost updates — mitigated with semantic locks or status flags); compensations are semantic, not inverse; every step must be idempotent because retries are guaranteed at-least-once; compensations must be idempotent and must not fail, so they retry forever into a dead-letter queue. Coordinate by choreography (events) or orchestration (a coordinator). The dual-write problem — commit plus publish — is solved with a transactional outbox.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.note: Gets a fast 'order accepted' — not 'order complete'. The saga is still running, and the UI has to be honest about that.

nodes.label: Saga orchestrator
nodes.note: Holds the saga's state machine: which step we are on, what to do on success, what to compensate on failure.

without: Three services each commit to their own database with no shared transaction
Step 3 fails after steps 1 and 2 committed: the customer is charged for an order that cannot ship
With no component tracking the sequence, nobody knows a half-finished order exists until a customer complains
with: Each step is a local ACID transaction that either commits or does not
A recorded saga state means a failure at step 3 triggers compensations for steps 2 and 1, in reverse
The whole flow is one readable state machine you can log, replay and debug
why.conclusion: You trade atomicity for eventual correctness plus an explicit, inspectable flow — the intermediate half-finished state becomes visible by design rather than by accident.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.note: T1: create order in PENDING. Compensation C1: mark it CANCELLED — a status change, not a delete, because the record is evidence.

nodes.label: Payment service
nodes.note: T2: charge the card. Compensation C2: issue a refund. The original charge still appears on the customer's statement — this is why a compensation is not a rollback.

nodes.label: Inventory service
nodes.note: T3: reserve stock. Fails here when the item sold out between the order and the reservation.

nodes.label: Outbox + relay
nodes.note: Each service writes its event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as its state change; a relay reads the table and publishes. Commit and publish can no longer half-happen.

without: Three services each commit locally, so a failure at the third leaves the first two committed: the customer is charged for an order that will never ship
There is no shared transaction to roll back and no component that knows the order was half-created, so the inconsistency is discovered by a customer, not by the system
Ad-hoc cleanup code appears in every caller, each handling a different subset of the failure cases and none of them handling a crash midway
Reaching for a distributed transaction instead couples the services' lifetimes together — if payment is down, orders cannot commit at all
with: Each step is a local ACID transaction that either commits or does not; no locks are held across services
A failure triggers compensations in reverse order, returning the system to a business-correct state
The saga's state is recorded, so a crash mid-flow resumes rather than losing the order
Services stay independently deployable and independently available
why.conclusion: A saga gives up atomicity and isolation to keep availability and independence — the system is briefly, visibly half-finished, and the design work is deciding what that looks like to a user.

whenToUse: A business process spans several services that each own their own database
The steps have meaningful compensations — a refund, a cancellation, a release of a reservation
Availability matters more than momentary consistency: it is better to accept the order and sort payment out than to refuse while payment is slow
Long-running flows where holding any lock for the duration would be absurd (a step waits on a human, a bank or a courier)
whenNotToUse: The data is all in one database — use a plain transaction; a saga there is pure cost and strictly weaker
A step genuinely cannot be compensated: you cannot un-send the email, un-ship the box or un-publish the public post, and 'we'll send an apology' is not an acceptable outcome for the case at hand
Intermediate states are unacceptable to read: if another process seeing a charged-but-unconfirmed order causes a second charge, you need real isolation, not semantic locks bolted on later
A two-step flow between services you control and could merge — the operational weight of a saga (state store, retries, dead letters, compensation tests) outweighs a boundary you drew arbitrarily
The team has no way to observe it: a saga you cannot trace end to end is an order that silently stops at step 3 forever

pros: Real atomicity across participants: all commit or all abort
No compensation logic to write, test or reason about
cons: Participants hold locks from prepare until commit — the whole cross-service round trip, not one local commit
If the coordinator dies after prepare, participants are blocked holding locks with no way to decide alone
Availability is the product of all participants': any one being down blocks everyone
Needs XA-style support that most modern datastores and queues simply do not offer

tradeoffs.option: Saga with choreography (services react to events)
pros: No central component to build, deploy or scale
Services stay loosely coupled — each only knows the events it emits and consumes
Adding a participant to a simple flow can mean just subscribing to an event
cons: The flow exists nowhere as written-down logic; you reconstruct it by reading every service's handlers
Past roughly four or five steps it becomes genuinely hard to answer 'what happens next?' or 'where did this order stop?'
Cyclic dependencies creep in as services start listening to each other's events
Compensation ordering is implicit, so a missed case is invisible until it fires in production

tradeoffs.option: Saga with orchestration (a coordinator drives the steps)
pros: The flow is one explicit state machine you can read, diagram, test and step through
Failure and compensation paths are written down in one place
Easy to answer 'where is order 12345?' — the saga state says so
Participants stay simple: they expose a command and its compensation and know nothing about the flow
cons: A new component that knows about every participant — a coupling point and a thing to keep available
Business logic drifts into the orchestrator until the services are anaemic
The orchestrator's own state must be durable and recoverable, or a crash strands sagas mid-flight

tradeoffs.option: Accept the inconsistency and reconcile in batch
pros: Almost no runtime machinery — a nightly job finds charged-but-unshipped orders and fixes them
Often the honest answer for low-volume, low-value flows
cons: The inconsistency is visible to users for hours, and they will contact support before the job runs
Reconciliation logic rots quietly because nothing exercises it until it is wrong

keyNumbers.label: Local ACID transaction
keyNumbers.value: ~1–10 ms — the thing you are giving up

keyNumbers.label: Typical saga completion, healthy path
keyNumbers.value: tens to hundreds of ms — the sum of every step, not the slowest

keyNumbers.label: Compensation window (charge to refund issued)
keyNumbers.value: seconds to minutes in the system; the refund itself may take days to clear at the bank

keyNumbers.label: Choreography comprehension limit
keyNumbers.value: roughly 4–5 steps before nobody can follow the flow

keyNumbers.label: Outbox relay lag
keyNumbers.value: sub-second with polling in the ~100 ms–1 s range; near-immediate with log tailing

keyNumbers.label: Delivery guarantee every step must survive
keyNumbers.value: at-least-once — assume every message arrives twice

quiz.question: Why is two-phase commit rarely chosen for a microservice flow, despite giving true atomicity?
options: It cannot handle more than two participants
It holds locks across services for the whole round trip, and a coordinator crash after prepare leaves participants blocked with no way to decide
It is slower than a saga by roughly an order of magnitude on the happy path
It requires all participants to share one database
quiz.explanation: The blocking case is the killer. After a participant votes to prepare it has promised it can commit and must hold its locks until told which way — if the coordinator dies, it cannot decide alone, so it waits, holding locks, while unrelated traffic queues behind them. Raw latency is not the objection; availability is. 2PC makes your system's uptime the product of every participant's.

quiz.question: Your payment service commits the charge to its database and then publishes a PaymentCompleted event. The process crashes between the two. What is this problem called and what is the standard fix?
options: Split brain; use a consensus cluster to elect one publisher
The dual-write problem; use a transactional outbox — write the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the state change, and let a separate relay publish from that table
A lost update; wrap the publish in a retry loop
Head-of-line blocking; move the publish to a separate partition
quiz.explanation: Writing to your database and publishing to a broker are two independent operations, so they can partially fail in either direction — money taken but nobody told, or an event for a charge that rolled back. A retry loop does not help; the crash is the point. The outbox makes the event part of the same atomic commit, and the relay's at-least-once publishing is fine precisely because every consumer is already idempotent.

quiz.question: Step 3 of a saga fails, so the orchestrator issues the compensation for step 2: refund the card. That refund call times out and is retried, and the compensation itself then fails permanently. What are the two design rules this scenario is testing?
options: Compensations must run in the original order, and only the last step needs a compensation

Compensations must be idempotent so a retried refund does not pay out twice, and they must be built never to fail permanently — retry with backoff and land in a dead-letter queue for a human, because there is no compensation for a compensation
Compensations should be skipped if the forward step has already been acknowledged
Compensations must hold a lock on the payment record until the saga completes
quiz.explanation: A timeout does not tell you whether the refund happened, so it will be retried — without idempotency (a key on the refund request), the customer is paid twice. And nothing exists downstream of a compensation to clean it up: if C2 can fail and be forgotten, the money is simply gone. The working pattern is infinite retry with backoff plus a dead-letter queue and an alert, so a person resolves what the system cannot. Compensations run in reverse order, and every completed step needs one.
